utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. There are several matters that I would like to deal with before we resume hearing the witness. On 10th of November, 2011, during the testimony of KDZ011, the Chamber admitted Exhibit D1911 into evidence and marked D1912 for identification. Subsequently, Ms. Sutherland orally requested the Chamber to reconsider admitting the two documents. Given that D1912 was only MFI'd, the Chamber considers Ms. Sutherland's intervention as an objection to the admission of this document and not as a request for reconsideration of the decision to admit it. The Chamber recalls that D1911 is a 1991 Banja Luka security services report discussing events in Croatia and how they affected the "security situation" in municipalities in BiH along the border, including in KDZ011's municipality of Bosanski Novi. The Chamber notes that KDZ011 gave testimony about the presence of Muslim police officers in Suhaca, Bosanski Novi, and stated that in the municipality of Bosanski Novi there were rumours about the situation in Croatia as well as a fear that fighting would "spill over" into Bosnia. The Chamber thus considers that sufficient foundation was laid for the admission of the document and therefore that the Prosecution has not demonstrated the existence of a clear error in reasoning or that of particular circumstances justifying that the admission decision be reconsidered in order to prevent an injustice. With regard to MFI D1912, purportedly a "security situation assessment in Bosanski Novi" from 16th of April, 1992, the Chamber notes that it currently lacks an English translation of the document so cannot verify its contents. The Chamber thus considers that any objection relating to its admission, including whether a proper foundation was laid for its admission, may be considered once an English translation has been received and the Chamber proceeds with examining whether the document should be admitted. Next, the Chamber will issue its decision on the status of the annexes to the accused's 61st motion for finding of disclosure violation related to Mevludin Sejmenovic and the accused's supplemental memorandum in support of 60th motion for finding of disclosure violation related to Ivo Atlija, both filed on 26th of October, 2011. The Chamber considered the Prosecution's notification filed on 8th of November, 2011, and noted the passage on which the parties agreed and those on which it disagreed and in relation to which the Prosecution submits that they relate to the witness's co-operation with the Prosecution and their privacy and security. The Chamber notes that witnesses Atlija and Sejmenovic are not the subject of protective measures and that there is therefore no reason to redact information related to their co-operation with the Prosecution or the reasons for which they were seeking residence in a third country. The Chamber therefore orders the accused to refile the 61st motion for finding of disclosure violation and the supplemental memorandum in support of 60th motion for finding of disclosure violation of 26th of October, 2011, with public redacted versions of confidential Annex A to the accused's 61st motion and of confidential Annex B to the accused's supplemental memorandum in accordance with the redactions agreed upon by the parties and identified in yellow in the Prosecution's submission of 8th of November, 2011. The Chamber further orders the Registry to reclassify the 61st motion and the supplemental memorandum of 26th of October, 2011, to the effect that the respective annexes therein are made confidential. That said, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Unless there are other matters to deal with, we'll bring in the witness. In the meantime, I think we -- I received the spreadsheet you referred to, which seems to be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I just also wanted to say that we have uploaded a redacted version of the expert report, taking out the section which were struck, and that's 11 -- 117A. It should be in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we also find the spreadsheet helpful and it might be useful. We don't have any objection if the Trial Chamber receives those kind of materials in advance of the expert witness's testimony in the future. I think that would help things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your kind understanding. That would be helpful indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies for keeping you waiting, but there are several matters to deal with before we start today. Very well. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we continue where we broke off on Friday, I would like to ask you something. Are you familiar with our laws and our political system?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an area of my expertise that's covered in this report. I'm aware of some of the laws, such as the Law on National Defence, but it's not an area that I am an expert on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, on page 102, lines 122 to 123, you objected and said that I did not get up and tell an MP that he was not supposed to be saying something that he was saying. So that's what you said on Friday. It's in the transcript from page 112 to 123. Do you know that the speaker of the Assembly -- or, rather, the president does not sit throughout Assembly hearings all the time?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unaware one way or the other whether he sits through the Assembly session all the time. It would seem that you certainly spoke at this Assembly session and delegates followed you, and it would seem that the decisions being taken at that Assembly session, in particular the establishment of the army, the Presidency, the issues of the strategic goals, were quite -- quite important. But in answer to your question, I -- I can't say whether or not the speaker of the Assembly sits through the hearings at all time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The president of the republic. My question had to do with the president of the republic, actually. The president of the republic, does he have to sit at all Assembly sessions or not? What I'm putting to you is that that is not case and if he is there, he's not there for very long, and he can leave the session and take care of other business; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have no view one way or the other. I assume anyone can leave the Assembly session. It wasn't indicated in the minutes, certainly of that Assembly session, that, for example, yourself or Mr. Krajisnik, who I know certainly talked at the end of the session, seemed to have left, but, of course, anyone can leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the president of the republic cannot be involved in the upbringing and education of MPs because they're elected, too, and therefore the president does not have the right to reprimand them or caution them or try to educated them in any way?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the regulations may be in relation to formal education or otherwise of delegates or members, but my point on Friday was that I didn't see in the minutes of this discussion you indicating to the delegates that what they were talking about was unacceptable or that they had clearly misread what you had said in relation to the strategic objectives. There doesn't seem to be any language at all in that session, and I -- I at least am left, when I read the minutes, that the delegates took what you told them at the beginning of that session, put their points forward, some of them indicating -- discussing the issue of resettlement, and that there was no interjection by you nor Mr. Krajisnik in relation to the fact that they seem to have got a mis -- the wrong idea about -- about what was expected of them in the coming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to give me answers that are as brief as possible. Now I'm going to tell you what it's like in our political system. The president of the republic does not have to sit there at Assembly sessions. The president of the republic can intervene in parliamentary proceedings by refusing to sign a bill and turn it into a law. If a bill goes back to parliament, if the Assembly votes with a two-third majority, then the president has to sign that bill and turn it into a law. Are you aware of that kind of thing in political systems?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not my area of expertise, and I am not aware of that type of regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Brown, you are saying what the president was supposed to do, and I'm telling you what the president can do. But all right, let me ask you this now: You focused on many individual statements made by the MPs. Were you following what had happened? Did such positions prevail? Did they become part of Assembly documents, or did they just remain as a lone voice, as it were?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I've -- I've -- I quite follow the question. I haven't looked at the statements of the delegates and then taken them back to their own particular areas. It would seem that certainly in the case of Mr. Vjestica from Bosanska Krupa that he's talking about what had already happened, not what was necessarily going to be happening in the weeks. But to answer your question, I haven't -- I haven't followed, bearing in mind some of the delegates were from other areas outside the Krajina, but I didn't follow that. That wasn't really within the remit of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just conclude with dealing with your reference to the Assembly. I'm going to put to you the Defence case now. The Assembly meets to produce one of seven types of documents - the constitution, laws, resolutions, declarations, decisions, conclusions, and recommendations. Do you agree that the Assembly cannot meet with no reason whatsoever and that the reason for the Assembly to meet is the production of legislative documents? Just like in your country, after all.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, from the minutes that I did review it would seem that there were decisions, there was discussion, there were resolutions in relation to the circumstances at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you found a document of the Assembly where an extremist view prevailed and that I should have refused to sign?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I would have to go through all of the Assembly sessions, and I think there were a few of them, and it wasn't necessarily a key area of my report, but I think that there was a lot of language in this -- in these -- in the Assembly sessions, and I can draw your attention to some of them, the 16th Assembly session, in particular, which seemed to be quite inflammatory, possibly even derogatory, and I'm not sure necessarily would have aided to a calming of the situation at the time. But, again, the study of all the aspects of the Assembly sessions were not a key component of the report. I do know, and I think I said last week, or I do believe, that the 16th Assembly session was not an isolated, stand-alone Assembly session. There are references from what I remember in some of the previous minutes to the controlling of some of the territory that was highlighted by you, Mr. Karadzic, in relation to the strategic goals. There was discussion in particular in some of the Assembly sessions in March, or discussion and decisions, about taking control, establishing TOs. So the Assembly session on the 16th -- the 16th Assembly session was a stand-alone one, but in relation to your question about extremism, I think there are references in those Assembly sessions certainly with inflammatory language and derogatory language. I can draw your attention to some of them at the 16th Assembly session, because I do have the minutes of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm asking you now, Mr. Brown, and you probably know that. In our system, an MP cannot be held responsible for something he said from the rostrum; however, this is what I'm asking you now: Did extremist views prevail, and did they become part of the Assembly documents? And also, did you see for yourself that I intervened when I saw that an extremist view was about to prevail, but I did not respond to each and every particular contribution to the discussions? Now, that was one question. My next question: Is it true that you selectively looked at this thing or that from the Assembly but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, put your question one by one. One at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember you interjecting in relation to the issue of extremist views. Maybe at the 16th Assembly session you're able to point out to me where you've done that, because it's not my reading of the minutes. I certainly accept that these are minutes, but I don't see it, in certainly in the minutes of the 16th Assembly session, where you interject in relation to phrases or comments from some of the delegates that could be seen as inflammatory. If they are there, maybe you could point them out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the contribution of such delegates incorporated into the documents? Have you come across any such documents, and did the Assembly adopt their views as its own?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an area of my expertise. I did not look at the decisions of the Assembly. That was dealt with, I believe, by others within the leadership research team. All I can say, as I argue in my report, in particular in relation to the issue of separation, that the military -- there are a number of references in the military documents about separation. For example, one of the documents we saw last week in which the -- not long after this Assembly session, in which the Krajina Corps indicated that those leaving were not going to be returning. But as to the decisions themselves that you talk about, it's not an area of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. We'll come to that. Please look at your paragraph 1.43 in which you imply that again the issue of territories and my views about that issue is something where you quote as follows: [In English] "... do not want to get a state which has a huge number of those who are against that state ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you are interpreting this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify the para number again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.43, footnote 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So here the Trial Chamber has already seen and admitted into evidence several decisions and orders that I issued and that were adopted after this particular session that would pertain to the civilians from other ethnic communities. Between April and December, 1992, I issued some 20 orders in which I ordered and appealed for the protection of members of other ethnic communities. The majority of them have been admitted into evidence, and I can show them to you. Now, have you seen these documents and have you taken them into account? 65 ter, for example, 1083; 65 ter 1910; 65 ter 1116. Nearly all of them have been admitted into evidence. 65 ter 10537, 65 ter 11100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How can the witness follow your question? One at a time again. Before seeing the documents, can you answer the question, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't seen those documents, Your Honour. They may well have been issued. The 1st Krajina Corps issued certain instructions which I've noted in the report, such as abiding by the Geneva Conventions and others. But certainly issuing documents is one thing, and having those implemented or seeing if anything at all resulted from those documents is another. I think I stand by my assertions in paragraph 1.43.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brown, isn't it up to the Trial Chamber to decide what kind of documents these are? Have you made any reference to these documents, and did you draw it to the attention of the trial that there is this side of the story as well? Why didn't you present these documents to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, he said he hasn't seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I have to call up those documents, although it's going to be a waste of time. Can we have, please, D00426.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before? It's dated the 8th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's too small, we can only have an English version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember seeing this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 1090, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karadzic, when witness said that he hadn't seen any of these documents, there's no point of putting those documents to the witness. You can use them later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think he said he didn't know whether he had seen them before. So I think for -- in those circumstances I don't know what else we could do besides show them to him. Because, if he didn't see them, I think that affects the completeness of his report. And if he did see them and didn't include them, that also could have some implications unless he's given a chance to explain why not. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's do that as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, have you seen the letter that I wrote to Mr. Boutros-Ghali on the 13th of June in which I say that we denounce the paramilitary groups, that we outlaw them, and that we agreed with any sanctions imposed against them?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before. However, on the brief reading that I've just done of the document, it would seem to at least sit with a document later on that the Main Staff pushed out in relation to paramilitary groups. It says here in this document: "We want to inform you about our latest official decision to disown all paramilitary groups that are not ready to be under our political control." There was a document which is referenced in my report which is a large document from the Main Staff, it may even be a little bit later than that this document, relating to the issue of paramilitaries, identifying a large number of paramilitary groups that were operating on RS territory. And in order to control those paramilitary groups, it's advocated the placing of those groups into the ranks of the VRS, and only then if they refused that were they to be disbanded or dealt with. It would seem at least -- I would have to put the other documents together, but it would seem at least this document here, there's a qualification that it's not relating to all paramilitary groups irrespective of what they've done previously; it's relating to paramilitary groups that are not ready to be under the -- "our" or the RS leadership's or the RS authorities' political control. It seemed to echo somewhat of a theme that paramilitaries in RS territory were accepted as long as they were under the control or authority of the formal VRS military. And this doesn't say all paramilitary groups irrespective of what they've done in the past will be dealt with. I think this potentially echos a policy that -- that seemed to, say, be a thread that paramilitary groups were tolerated no matter what they'd done and would only not be tolerated if they refused to be put under army control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have an objection to the translation into Serbian. This should be translated as "We are giving up on them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, we are imparting here a piece of information that we are going to prosecute those who were not under our control. Do you know that we arrested and convicted all the groups that refused to subject themselves to the control of the military and the police? This Chamber is well aware of such cases. Are you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may well have been some paramilitaries that were prosecuted because they refused to come under the control of the army. I'm not necessarily aware of them off the top of my head. I believe there might have been one group in Doboj, but I'd have to go back and look at that. But it strikes me as the reason they were prosecuted was more of an issue of control and their refusal to come under the control of the RS authorities, that there didn't seem to be a reason or a belief that paramilitaries should be prosecuted for the crimes they committed. As a former military officer, having any paramilitaries who've committed crimes in your ranks strikes me as being, first and foremost, wrong, having criminals in the military. And secondly, if paramilitaries are committing crimes and known to have committed crimes, there's a whole issue of military control. Why would you want to include those individuals in -- in a professional military? My view, I think, reading some of the documents in relation to paramilitaries is that they were accepted as long as they were in the military. It didn't matter what they'd done. And they were only not accepted if they refused to come under the control of the military. The solution was about getting control of them rather than one of a criminal justice issue of prosecuting people who had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, your answers are much too elaborate. I would have enjoyed them immensely had I had enough time. Now, let me ask you this: Did you analyse how our judicial system operated, and did you find that there was any instance in which a group that had committed a war crime evaded Prosecution? Was that also a part of your remit?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't part of the remit I set myself when I wrote the report. There were a very small number of incidents very much at the low level that I did see in the Banja Luka area. I think there was an incident in Kljuc or Sanski Most municipality, I forget, in which low-ranking soldiers were prosecuted for an incident. It may well have been the school in Kljuc or it may have been two incidents. These are the only ones I really remember. In relation to the prosecution of soldiers for war crimes, I did not see that in -- in any significance at all. And even when there was incidences in the Krajina Corps reports clearly indicating that there'd been criminal activity, I did not see the prosecution of members of the Krajina Corps. For example, in the incident in Vecici in November 2000 -- 1992, where daily combat reports of the corps -- or a daily combat of the corps [sic] reported the massacre of captured members from the village of Vecici by members of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, I saw no investigation on that. I did not see any reference in the documents I reviewed that the commander of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade was investigated or prosecuted, nor did I see the operations group commander above him investigated or prosecuted, nor did I see any staff member of the 1st Krajina Corps, nor General Talic, investigated or prosecuted. And I -- and there are other examples of either retaliatory action or -- which is referenced in the Krajina Corps, involving the killing of individuals, and I never saw any senior commander in the Krajina Corps being prosecuted for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you never saw any evidence to the effect that our courts did operate and did their job. Did you seek to find such evidence? And can you please give me short answers. Did you look for this particular evidence, and was the subject of your expert report the sanctioning of the crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not objecting. I just want to -- I do object, actually, to the constant calls to make -- for the witness to make his answers shorter. The witness is giving fairly nuanced answers to some complex questions and trying to explain his answers carefully, so I don't think these have been unfairly long answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware of material taken from the Banja Luka Military Court and was able to review that material. I didn't see anything in that material, apart from a small number - and I'd have to go back in the details, it was a long time ago - a small number of cases very much at the low level, and I think only in two areas. I think one in Sanski Most and this incident in Kljuc. And even reviewing those materials, it didn't seem that there was any substantive punishment or follow -- follow-through with the investigation. So in answer to your question did I look for it, yes. In reviewing the materials that was seized from the Banja Luka Military Court, did I see any significant prosecutions for war crimes? No. General Talic remained as the corps commander until the end of the war and afterwards, and in fact, I believe, became commander of the VRS. And I didn't see any examples of brigade or senior-level commanders in the Krajina Corps being prosecuted or investigated even, I believe, for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, are you a jurist?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what the question is, but a jurist, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But as an officer, you know that a commander can be prosecuted for having ordered something or for failing to undertake preventive measures before the fact or prosecution measures after the fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just an officer, Mr. Karadzic. I believe it's members of the -- of the VRS. But, yes, it's not just the fact that they order something, but they fail to take steps to prevent it or do nothing afterwards having known that an incident has occurred. I'm not an expert on RS law, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you find any officer from the 1st Krajina Corps who have done something like that, that he either committed a crime or failed to prevent it or failed to take steps and that he avoided prosecution? Can you show us any specific document that would show this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I can highlight documents from the 1st Krajina Corps that reference incidents that would seem to be of a criminal nature. The daily combat report, I believe it's on the 4th of November, in relation to Vecici and Kotor Varos claims that there was a massacre of captured prisoners from Vecici by members of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade. There was a reference - and I'd have to look at my report - off the top of my head, in relation to Celinac. I believe it references the Celinac Light Infantry Brigade as killing, I believe, five Muslims in -- as reprisals for an event that had occurred somewhere else against VRS soldiers. I am aware of a reference from Manjaca camp in which a prisoner was beaten to death, Omer Filipovic, and -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, was the perpetrator of this particular crime ever tried?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the question opened the door to the references that you can tell us where there was a failure to prevent or punish or prosecute, and the witness was answering the question of those cases he's remembered. It's not fair to cut him off just because perhaps Mr. Karadzic didn't like the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Do you wish to continue, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only to conclude that in those three examples that I remember, I do not see any references to the 1st -- the 1st Krajina Corps collection, nor do I remember in the Banja Luka Military Courts commander of the 1st -- the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade being prosecuted for -- or -- or members of his brigade. I don't remember the Celinac Light Infantry Brigade commander, nor members of his brigade, being prosecuted. I do not remember the camp commander at Manjaca, Colonel Popovic, being held accountable for the prisoners under his care, and he certainly was in his -- in position as camp commander at the end of 1992 when the camp was closed after the release of all the prisoners that we talked about last week. I mean, those are three examples that I know. And I certainly don't see any of the staff officers of the Krajina Corps being held accountable for the actions of those in those brigades. There may be other examples in the report, but those are the ones I remember off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Brown, this is not the answer to my question. My question was, have you ever found any document in which the Krajina Corps issued an order to commit a crime or issued an order to cover up a crime? If in their combat report they report about crimes being committed, you can't call it a cover-up; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe if I break your question down. Do I know of any documents in which the Krajina Corps issued an order to commit a crime. I'm not sure I do. I'd have to go and look at all the footnotes, but I'm not sure I do. Do I know of any documents which indicate to me that they tried to cover up a crime. Yes. In particular, the Vecici killings in Kotor Varos in November. There's a series of documents discussing this incident, and it's reported as a brutal massacre by members of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade on one day, and the following day is reported in a combat report as combat casualties. And bearing in mind that I didn't see anyone from the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade investigated, from the documents I reviewed and was able to review, one could draw the conclusion that they knew a massacre had happened against prisoners who had been captured from the village of Vecici. It was initially reported that it was a brutal massacre, highlighting the unit that had been involved in that massacre, and then the following day reported as combat casualties, and the subsequent senior commanders were never replaced, as far as I'm aware, as a result of that incident. So, yes, that is one. There are other references in the Krajina Corps documents about -- well, probably -- almost one last week about the -- thank goodness the international community didn't hear about the killing on Mount Vlasic. So -- but certainly in the Kotor Varos case, I would classify that as something of a cover-up. If I may add, also, that it may well be that in relation to Manjaca there was a knowledge, at least looking at the documents -- some of the documents from Manjaca, that there was an awareness that conditions were poor, people were being -- individuals were being abused, that many people in there didn't deserve to be there, and yet during the visits of the ICRC, Mr. Mazowiecki, for example, there seemed to be an indication that, you know, "We're not going to --" that these people are here on some other mission and there is no admission that those conditions -- or about those conditions. So whether that's a cover-up or just being not -- not being completely honest about the conditions there, I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you see, I'll try to put simple questions. I'll cite an example of Manjaca. There the warden or the commander or one of his men sent a letter to the municipality saying that they had people there who had not taken part in combat, and he said he had no documents about them, and yet we had a witness here from Manjaca who confirmed that these documents were late. Do you understand that from Vecici and from Manjaca that the first information received may well be inaccurate, and by the time a second report is in the pipeline the information is already much more accurate? Do you understand that possibility? If you read a first report which says that there are some people who shouldn't be detained and, by the token of the same report, additional documentation is sought, have you ever had occasion to see a second report as a follow-up advising on the arrival of the requested documentation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that -- that may well be the case, but certainly in the documents that I was shown in relation to Manjaca it wasn't just one reference. There were a number of references. And there are a number of references in the 1st Krajina Corps reports also indicating to the Main Staff that -- maybe it's not specific to Manjaca, but in detention centres there are many people who didn't deserve to be there. There is a document at the end of August, 22nd of August, which is sent from the forward command post to Prijedor, something of an intelligence report, which discusses -- it's referenced in my -- my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the details.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, do not interrupt the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document which is referenced in my report, dated the 22nd of August, discussing the issue of camps in the Prijedor area, and they indicate that individuals are washing their hands of detention centres and passing -- attempting to pass on responsibility for the killing of Muslims, or civilians, and the ordering of the killing of civilians in those camps, and this document also makes mention that they're in essence feeling the cost of what they call the needless spilling of blood and the incarceration of individuals who didn't deserve to be there or at least who took no -- who had done nothing against the Serbian state. So it's not just one or two Manjaca documents that indicate that there were individuals in those detention centres who didn't deserve to be there. Some of those references found their way into the main -- 1 Krajina Corps daily combat reports and were sent up to the Main Staff. And there are other documents, including this one of the 22nd of August, which seems to imply that it is known externally to the corps that there are many people in the detention camps, some who have been killed, who had not taken any -- or who were not against the Serbian state and yet they were still in those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you found it in the documents of the 1st Krajina Corps which went from the lower-ranking units up to the Main Staff. Would you call that covering up? Yes or no? I guess you can answer in that way.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the Vecici, certainly it went to the Main Staff. Nothing seems to have happened. Nothing came back down from the Main Staff. There was no apparent obvious investigation from the documents that I saw. In relation to Manjaca camp, was it closed because of the conditions and because of the knowledge that large numbers of people didn't deserve to be there? No. It was closed at the end of the year, some five or six months after it was established. It's not for me to say whether it's a cover-up particularly. All I can say is this seems to be what the document said. In a number of cases there were specific examples of killings of non-Serbs by identified units in the 1st Krajina Corps. And that's aside from other references more generic about destruction of property or movements out of individuals. But there were some specific examples identifying units that have been involved in killings in which I did not see anyone being prosecuted. I leave it to others to decide whether that's couched as a cover-up or whatever. All I'm saying is this is what I saw from some of the documents in the Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I say, Mr. Brown, that your knowledge as regards that is basically none. Why should Colonel Popovic be tried for Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, Dr. Karadzic. It's not for me to decide why or what someone might be tried for. All I'm saying in relation to Manjaca was that it was established by the 1st Krajina Corps. It received a large number of prisoners predominantly from other detention sites, such as Omarska and some in Sanski Most. It was commanded and run by Colonel Popovic under the auspices of the 1st Krajina Corps. The documents that I've reviewed indicate that conditions were poor, that it was known by the Krajina Corps that conditions were poor. It was known that a large number of people in Manjaca didn't deserve to be there. There are other indications that beatings took place. And certainly in the case of Omer Filipovic, not long after an ICRC visit he was beaten to death. The ICRC report reported and quoted in a 1st Krajina Corps document that conditions were poor, that they saw fresh traces of blood, they weren't allowed to speak to all the people that they asked to, and that they had concerns about the camps and the prisoners within it. I'm aware from the Krajina Corps that Mr. Mazowiecki, who was there, from the documents, at least, on a humanitarian mission and presumably being a senior UN figure, had wanted to visit the camp. It must have come to his attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must interrupt you. I apologise. My question was specific. Why do you refer in today's transcript twice to the fact that Colonel Popovic was not tried? What crime was he, according to you, supposed to have been tried? You mentioned Omer Filipovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, he was explaining the reason why he referred to Colonel Popovic. Please continue, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Popovic, Your Honours, was the commander of that camp, and he came under the authority of the 1st Krajina Corps. The contextual background I've highlighted in relation to Manjaca camp is from the documents that I've seen from the 1st Krajina Corps. And based on those documents it would strike me that at best Colonel Popovic had a case to answer about the conditions in that camp, the treatment of the prisoners over an extended period, for others to decide whether that is accurate, what law may apply, but it would strike me, as my experience, that a former officer, on looking at the documents, that Colonel Popovic certainly had a case to answer in relation to Manjaca camp, the conditions there that were known through the documents that I've reviewed, contemporaneous, 1st Krajina Corps documents. And it may not be just Colonel Popovic. Colonel -- Colonel -- Major-General Talic sat above him. And, again, it may be for others to decide, but it strikes me there's at least a case to answer that that camp was not a healthy place to be. He ran it, and he was aware that conditions were poor and that bad things were going on inside that camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, Mr. Karadzic, we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I put just one question. We haven't run the course of the full 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, did you know that at Manjaca there were only two cases of death, three due to natural causes and two were violent deaths, and that in the case of those two violent deaths people were prosecuted? Did you know that the killer of Omer Filipovic was called to -- be called before a court?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. That certainly didn't seem to be the case in 1992. It may well have been the case a long time afterwards. But it's not solely the fact that Filipovic and one other were killed there, but that conditions were poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I'm not asking you that. Your desire to expand, Mr. Brown, will result in your testimony lasting for a week. Please answer my questions. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the witness is answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- are biased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's not a question. That's an accusation. Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, if you ask elaborate questions of an expert witness, you are going to get elaborate answers. The first rule of cross-examination, as Mr. Robinson will no doubt tell you, is do not ask a question to which you do not want to know the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was simple: Did he know they were prosecuted, that the killers were tried? Why would Popovic have to stand a trial when the killers did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, put your question one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I asked. I was just trying to explain Judge Morrison that my question was simple. May we have this admitted, the one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether witness answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said he didn't take this document into account. That's not for me. He should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you didn't know that anybody was prosecuted for what happened in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And we are talking about 65 ter 1090, Mr. Karadzic. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1933, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for 25 minutes and resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to get back to you as quickly as possible regarding your inquiry concerning KDZ084 and the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought we began in -- my big mistake -- my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thanks to the kind understanding and co-operation of the Haradinaj Chamber, we have become able to sit in the morning tomorrow, as well as on the morning of Monday, 28th of November, next week. So I appreciate it very much. Let's bring in the witness. And as we discussed during the private session, we will interpose the next witness's evidence with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I have to inquire of you, Mr. Brown. Due to some circumstances regarding the next witness, we have just decided to interpose her evidence with your evidence. We expect to be able to finish your evidence tomorrow, but there may be a possibility that you have to stay till Thursday. Would it be okay with you, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be a pleasure, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your kind understanding. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'm an amateur in matters of law, and therefore I do find it easy to believe that my questions are not sufficiently focussed. In any case, I would still like to ask you to answer as briefly as possible, and I will try to be more focused. In paragraph 1.43, you said that, generally speaking: [As read] "... Karadzic was discussing the separation of members of different ethnicities in Bosnia-Herzegovina (as opposed to potential -- a potential division between the ethnic communities in the newly created Serbian state) ..." In other words, you are aware of the fact that it was one thing to separate the ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and another to separate them in Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that there can be two -- two questions, one which is the division of Bosnia into separate states and one of the separation of the communities within RS territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before you go further, I have to make a correction from my statement. We'll be sitting in the afternoon next week, Monday, not in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that I clearly indicated that movements of population are mandatory in the territory of the SRBiH, and you add that I said, We do not want to get a state which has a huge number of those who are against that state. Further below, you explain that certain deputies mentioned Sweden and Norway. I'll go back to the first part -- no, the second part first. Did you know that before the war there was a suggestion for the entire Yugoslavia, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, that a so-called model of the Scandinavian states should be introduced, and were you aware of what such a model would entail?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, maybe if I break your question up because there are a number of issues here. I don't say it's -- in this -- in the paragraph that movements of populations are mandatory in the territory. I say: "Although, at face value, it may have appeared that Karadzic was discussing the separation of the national groupings within Bosnia and Herzegovina more widely (as opposed potentially to the separation of ethnic groups in the new Serb state) he clearly did indicate that resettlement from within the SRBiH territory would be required. Karadzic, himself, declared that 'We do not want to get a state which has a huge number of those who are against that state' ..." And I believe there is at least another one reference on a similar -- in a similar area that you make. The second section. I am not aware of a model of Scandinavian states would be introduced into -- into Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina. All I'm saying is that the delegate who makes reference to that, I believe, made reference - I'd have to check the notes again - to the fact that the separation, I think in Sweden -- between Sweden and Norway took a long time, and the resettlement of the population as part of that took a long time. But in relation to your second question about was I aware of this model of Scandinavian states should be introduced, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were official proposals at the level of Yugoslavia that Scandinavisation be carried out, i.e., that we part ways the way the Scandinavian countries did and that borders be arranged as well as a certain period of time be left to those who wished to opt which country they wanted to reside in. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday we discussed the fact that you noticed I was against megalomania in territorial terms. My proposition now is this: When I said that we cannot have a state with many living in it who are against it, it was actually my recommendation that we should be more modest in terms of territorial requests. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly agree, from the reading of the minutes, that there are delegates who want significantly larger territory and that you caution against that. And I believe there might even be other references outside this Assembly session to that -- to that effect. I'll leave the issue of modesty to others, but it would seem that others were wanting more and that you were advocating against that in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a sentence here which I dispute. Apparently you say that I stated that there should be movements of population in the territory of the SRBiH. Did it only entail Republika Srpska or was this supposed to mean that people were to be moved from the RS to the other two entities and back?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the 16th Assembly session there's reference that Serbs inside BiH territory will -- this resettlement process will include the Serbs being -- being moved into -- into the territory of the RS, and I think there's even a reference by one of the delegates that we should be prepared for that and make preparations because it will involve people moving away from their -- their hearths or their territory. It's also of note, I think, that General Mladic, at the end when he speaks, certainly makes two references, it would appear, to indicate that he himself sees what is being discussed is about the movement of the population. In that way he says that people are not keys in pockets that can be moved from one place to another. I think he makes a reference to that people are not like a sieve, where some can fall through and others stay. And he warns, or appears to warn from the minutes, that, you know, what is going to be -- I think his phrase is genocide, actually. So in answering your question, it isn't simply about the movement of population within RS territory. I think there is an expectation that Serbs inside BiH territory will move into RS territory. And there are other references in documents which seem to indicate that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read this intercept of my conversation with Mr. Milosevic, President Milosevic, where I say that some Croat representatives suggested that the population be resettled, and I said that that was nebulous and a terrible thing that had to be avoided?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that intercept, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see my press conference on the 3rd of May when I returned from the Brussels conference and when I was asked by journalists what would happen with the borders of those who will not be within their own units, whether there's going to be resettlement, and I said we do not envisage, nor do we recommend resettlement; we propose reciprocal protection of rights? Have you seen that press conference, and have you included it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen the press conference. I would like to see it. And it is not included in the report. What was stated in the press, if that's an accurate depiction, I do not see replicated in the -- certainly the 16th Assembly session and some of the other military documents that I've reviewed. It may well be that what was being discussed in the press was for one audience and what was being discussed elsewhere was for another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this comment is out of order. Why does every sentence have to be repeated on each and every occasion, Mr. Brown? This is a publicly stated view of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1410, page 21, towards the bottom of the page. Twenty-one in e-court and then the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since there is no translation, allow me to read it out to you. "At the press conference, in response to a question put by the journalist, How many people should be resettled if there were to be a final separation, Dr. Karadzic answered, 'We have not been counting on resettlement, nor do we recommend that. According to our calculations, only 12 to 15 per cent of the population on every side would remain outside the borders of there respective communities. We suggest that they be protected on the basis of a principle of reciprocity and that they enjoy all rights enshrined in international conventions. As for application and protection of that right, the European institutions would take care of that in a role of a supervisor.'" And that was published in the "Borba" newspaper --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this position of mine?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this media statement, Mr. Karadzic, and I can only say that this would not seem to be what happened in the days and weeks and months after this statement, if that's a statement that was made in early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if I tell you that there was not and single place in Republika Srpska where there were no Muslims and that there were entire villages that no one had touched, what do you say to that? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the ethnic breakdown of all the areas in the RS. I don't doubt that there may well have been some non-Serbs who stayed there for a period of time for whatever reason or -- but it would seem to be that a large number, a significantly large number in the Krajina area didn't, but I don't doubt that there were non-Serbs who -- who did stay, even through the -- the whole of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? This is from Smilja Avramov's book. I think that we've already displayed that. It's a quote from the "Borba" daily newspaper though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, can I hear from you on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at least it should be marked at the moment since we don't have a translation. I'd like to take a look at it first. The witness did comment on it and stated it didn't appear to be -- reflect what he saw happening and didn't know anything about it, but I don't have any strong objection to it coming in. I'm not sure why the actual article isn't submitted instead of a excerpt or summary. Or I don't know if it's -- if it's verbatim or reprint or what, so it's hard to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was my question as well, Mr. Karadzic. You couldn't locate "Borba" article?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My associates are looking for it. We'll get it some day. But at any rate, this is an historian, a lady who is world renowned, and she included this in her book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber will not receive this book. Even if -- suppose even if we have an English translation, we have -- we have no idea whether -- while we do not doubt the integrity of the author, but we are not sure whether she correctly reflected what you said in the media interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to take a look. I'm going to try to find the text in "Borba" that was quoted. I hope that then it can be received. Can we please go back to the previous document, the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this same paragraph do you agree that it says -- I mean this MP says, We do not have that solution in this option, the one that has to do with resettlement? Paragraph 1.43. I believe it's on the next page. [In English] "If it is a state border, it is -- intrinsically implies moving of a continent of population. Within the present option, we do not have this solution." [Interpretation] Isn't that right; that's what he said?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just look at the whole quote from Mr. Milojevic for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What it says here is "implies," goes without saying. That's what is said in respect of resettlement; right? And all of this is being said by the same man who referred to Norway and Sweden; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a different man, Mr. Karadzic. Professor Milojevic was the one who -- is footnote 58, and the man who talked about Sweden and Norway was, I believe, Trifko Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But that is what was stated there, We do not have this solution within the present option. Right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- that's what's in the minutes, but if you look at the whole quote and the whole reference to the paragraph, Professor Milojevic, he is saying -- in fact, maybe it's easier if I read it out. "I would like to suggest there is no doubt that there will be the option of war and then negotiations, that we cannot expect solutions from negotiations only, that negotiations can only represent a modification of the success at war and of war solutions, which implies that we would have to have a map of our own. A border agreed between the political and military leadership of our republic, one thoroughly assessed, and I might add, kept a secret. Divulge it to no one, but each and every general must know this border, and the political leadership should keep this map as a potential negotiating chip. But this map needs to be mastered within a closed circle of people, presented to the deputies, but it is -- but it probably should be kept secret. And secondly, because of the war option which was imposed on us, initially we had been discussing some more peaceful options. This way we aim for a state border. If it's a state border intrinsically implies moving a contingent of the population. Within the present option we do not have the solution." I think what he's saying is that if we continue to negotiate we won't have this solution of resettlement, but if we have the first option, which is war, we will decide what our borders are, we can keep those borders secret, we don't tell anyone, and we use it as a negotiating chip. And if we set those borders, that that will intrinsically imply the moving of people within those borders. I think that's what Professor Milojevic is stating when he spoke at the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Professor Milojevic is a professor of economics, an economist? He is not a member of parliament. He is an expert in economic affairs.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know details about Professor Milojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 9th of June, in spite of his advice that the envisaged borders be kept secret, we decided to send to the European Community, to the negotiators at the conference, the six strategic objectives and maps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that being sent to the European Community. I'm not aware that it would have been couched in those phrases. What does seem to be evident is that the goals were announced at the 16th Assembly session. It is possible that the meeting on the 6th of June in which there seem to be a plotting of borders in some detail may well have been the borders that were set in discussions in the European Community. But I'm not aware of the details and the political negotiations that went on with the European Community at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D428. Can we take a brief look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any insight into the transcripts of the meetings of the Presidency, the Assembly, the government? Have you seen these minutes, for instance? There's got to be a translation. Look at paragraph 10, to make public the strategic goals and map of the Serbian BH and to have this sent to the European Community.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the minutes. That may well have been the case. It would seem to, if that was true, seem to imply that the strategic goals were of some importance. And as I say, this comes three days after the meeting that's noted in Mladic's diary, which seems to be quite a significant or at least a long meeting. And at one stage there's briefing of a map and it would seem to be plotting out territory that could well be the footprint articulated in the strategic goals. That's what the minutes say. It may well be that they were sent to the European Community. But it does seem to me important that the strategic goals were that footprint that RS territory was to contain as articulated in those goals. And maybe they were sent to the European Community or it's referenced here because those were the goals that you wanted to achieve concurrently with what was going on with the VRS and in the international community with negotiations with the EC and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this map of Republika Srpska does not basically differ from the first map that was offered by Ambassador Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could these -- could this please be put on the ELMO. We haven't uploaded the map in colour, so could this please be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of February. On that date it was agreed that more or less this is what the units are going to look like. Mr. Brown, do you know where the rivers Una, Sava, Drina, and Neretva are here? Is it correct that Una is on the western border of this darker area, Sava on the north, Drina on the east, and Neretva in the middle?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, generically. It's been some time since I looked at a detailed map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but generically those rivers are in those areas that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that what is envisaged here are a few enclaves that do -- that are not contiguous? Cazinska Krajina, the Bihac pocket. Then in the middle, this white area, is Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc, Muslim municipalities, parts of Muslim municipalities, that is. Then over here, the Serb municipality in Ozren. And here by Sarajevo, east of Sarajevo, there is Romanija and Birac. In the Drina valley, there is Muslim territory. You know where the Drina is, don't you? It's on the very east.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know where the Drina River is. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just a second. Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. It's not clear to me what actually is being represented to be on this ELMO at the moment is ... the question was: "Do you know that this map of Republika Srpska does not basically differ from the first map that was offered by Ambassador Cutileiro?" I don't know what map we're looking at, unless we missed it, and what this is from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was published in "Glas" on the 23rd of February, whereas on the 22nd of February what was agreed upon was that this map is the basis for the building of the three entities. This map shows that the western boundaries of Republika Srpska are supposed to be on the Una, the northern ones on the Sava, the eastern ones on the Drina, and there is Muslim territory along the Drina River, and on the Neretva it is the southern border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So my question is: Do you see that the European Community recognised that the right bank of the Una is populated by Serbs and that the strategic objectives, except for the corridor, correspond to what is on this map, that there is no major difference in respect of what was already offered to us on the 22nd of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that's an explanation that Mr. Nicholls wanted. What -- Mr. Nicholls, could you be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not in evidence that this map was agreed to or represents what the European Union Community had recognised. It may be Mr. Karadzic's position that this map from the "Glas" newspaper reflects what was -- something -- I'm not sure exactly what's saying, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I'm not sure whether this is -- this document itself is "Glas" article also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then I misunderstood Mr. Karadzic. I thought he was saying this is -- we're looking at something from "Glas."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map that was published in all the media on the 23rd of February as the proposal of the European Community as a basis -- we have it in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tell us what document -- what this is -- this document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map that was published in the media the day after the agreement had been reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the book itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh. This is a survey of news published in "Glas." It's a chronology. But it's also contained in Lord Owen's book. We can find it in several books. It is an indubitable map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify the objection: That -- that doesn't alter the fact that Mr. Karadzic is putting a proposition to the witness as fact which has not been established -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We'll come to that later on, but I want to establish what this document is about. It is not a "Glas" newspaper article. It is a -- it may be a compilation of news, but I don't know what it is about. You should put a proper foundation to put your question to the witness. And then it's improper to -- to put the witness, which witness cannot confirm, such as the argument that this map has been agreed to, as Mr. Nicholls and Tieger indicated. Let us continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to tender this now. We have this in several documents. I'm just asking the witness whether he is aware that the first map that was offered to us recognised the boundaries on the Sava, Drina, Neretva, and Una and that was envisaged were enclaves that were not contiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the war, without the war, do you understand that we accepted this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it is -- I'm aware that, in relation to the negotiations in early 1992, the Cutileiro Plan and European Union negotiations suggested the cantonisement of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that those would be -- those cantons would be based on Bosniak, Croat, or Serb -- Serb areas and they -- that there was a map or maybe even a series of maps in relation to the negotiations around that period. The Cutileiro Plan, as I'm aware, allowed for those cantons to be -- to be administered in those areas with a weaker centralised Bosnian government. It may well have been that some of the boundaries of some of the cantons were along the rivers as you note, in part because some of the rivers are -- form the boundary between -- for example, Sava River forms a boundary between Croatia in part. The Drina in part forms a boundary with Serbia. So there are these national issues too. I do not believe that the strategic goals and the territory encompassed within those matched exactly the Cutileiro Plan at all. The Posavina was different. I believe the issue with Sarajevo was different. And the desire to control the whole of the Drina valley, as articulated in the strategic goals, seems different than the Cutileiro Plan. I don't know of the negotiations around the Cutileiro Plan, what was agreed, what was a proposal, what was accepted, and obviously it did not come to fruition, but I do not support your assertion that the strategic goals as articulated on the 12th of May were in some way simply a replication of the Cutileiro Plan. I would accept that some of the boundaries overlapped in both the Cutileiro Plan and the strategic goals, but not in entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, again, I kindly ask you to give answers that are as short as possible. Do you agree that the corridor was requested only once the war broke out? It is not on the first map. Do you agree? The request to have a corridor appeared only when the war broke out. If you look at the first map, you will see that there is no corridor. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, in relation to the Cutileiro map, from what I remember, that many of the corridor municipalities were Croat or Bosniak -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you a simple question. Did we request a corridor before the war, or did we put this forth as an imperative only after the war started? It's a simple issue. When did the corridor appear for the first time? It was on the 12th of May, as late as that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you requested as part of the Cutileiro map or the negotiations. I don't know what happened and whether Cutileiro themselves proposed that that was territory that actually was Croat. So whether you requested it in the Cutileiro negotiations, I have no idea. It may well be that you didn't, but it may well be that you did but that Cutileiro decided that based on the ethnicity of the corridor areas that was going to be a different cantonment. I don't know. There had been some references, I believe, in some of the Assembly sessions about the importance of the corridor area well before the 12th of May, and I would certainly accept that military events in the corridor area in March when the Croats took control of certain key areas did -- did mean that Bosnian Serbs were not in control of the corridor, and I mention that in the report. But I can't answer your question simply because I don't know the negotiations that went on around Cutileiro and whether you requested a corridor but it was denied to you or whether you accepted that that was going to be an area that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you don't know whether we did request it either. My question refers to the map. Do you know that in February we accepted the map without the corridor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It's not for the witness -- to testify whether you accepted or not. But, Mr. Brown, you confirm, can you not, that in the map itself that such corridors were not reflected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. It was cantoned, I believe, for Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Secondly, a moment ago you said that in our six strategic objectives we demanded the control of Podrinje. That is not correct. We wanted to have a soft border on the Drina, rather. That's what you said a minute ago, i.e., that you knew that the control of Podrinje was part of the six strategic objectives, and I'm telling you that that is not correct. We envisaged Muslim municipalities in Podrinje, and our third objective said that the border on the Drina should be soft one; in other words, there shouldn't be any border at all.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, I can only go by what is reported in the minutes of the session, and it says by you: "The third strategic goal is to establish a corridor on the Drina valley, that is, elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds. We are not -- we are on both sides of the Drina, and our strategic interest and living space are there. We now see a possibility for some Muslim municipalities to be settled along the Drina as enclaves in order for them to achieve their rights, but that belt along the Drina must basically belong to the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. As much as it is of strategic use for us, in a positive way it helps us by damaging the interest of our enemy in establishing a corridor which would connect them to the Muslim international and render this area permanently unstable." I accept that in this reference you countenance the possibility of Muslim enclaves. I don't believe in Cutileiro, in relation to the cantonment, that the Drina envisaged Muslim enclaves in that manner, but it would seem to me from the minutes of the session at least that you believe the Drina valley should be controlled and that you may allow for the existence of some Muslim enclaves in that area. Importantly not just because you wanted to control it but because it denied that area to -- to the enemy as noted here. And I think that looking at the Drina Corps document and operational directive 4 later on in the year, that that position of having enclaves appeared, at least from that series of documents, to have been removed. Because, in operational directive 4 there is the reference that the Drina Corps is to -- is to in essence exhaust the Muslim -- Muslims -- Muslim fighters and units in that area and remove them along with the civilian population. So it may well have been your position in -- on the 12th of May that you accepted there could be Muslim enclaves, but I think later in that year that position had changed. And I don't think your view at the 16th Assembly session is the same as the Cutileiro map that was discussed earlier that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you know that the Owen-Stoltenberg and the Vance-Owen Plans, both of which I accepted, envisaged Muslim enclaves in Podrinje? Yes or no? What is important to me is to find out what was the basis of your report. Did you take into account both the Owen-Stoltenberg -- Vance-Owen and Cutileiro Plan and that they both envisaged Muslim enclaves and that we accepted that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the Owen-Stoltenberg and Vance-Owen Plans, the negotiations that went on surrounding that. It was outside the scope of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
