utterances.text: Thank you. I promised to show you the transcript, for the sake of saving time, to the effect that in January or February, 1993, on the occasion of the Vance-Owen Plan, I explained what the notion of the Drina means and what this third strategic goal entailed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court, please -- we don't have time to watch the video-clip. Instead, can we have 1D4868. Can we please look at the time-line 02:24:12. Page 24 of 33. 24. We can remove the right-hand side. This is page 23. We need 24 -- yes, we do have 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see -- [no interpretation] [In English] "I think that borders in Europe will never be that important, even though they exist -- existence is necessary." [Interpretation] Can you please read it to yourself and look at what it says here, and I also ask all the parties in the proceedings to do the same. Please tell me once you've read it, and then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have page 31 of 33. Please look at 2 -- 24 [as interpreted] -- 45:28, where the Drina is being mentioned and where an explanation of this specific strategic goal is provided. Is it clear to you now that this is a reference to border restrictions rather than the unification with Serbia and the removal of the borders altogether? Did you know this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to read the whole document maybe, but I don't see too much of a difference between what was articulated with strategic goal number 3, that we need to control both sides of the border and this is our territory. I don't know when this statement of yours was articulated. It does seem to be that you're indicating that the strategic aims are still important and extant and that it seems to echo what you said in May 1992, that the Drina should be controlled and it was -- both sides of the border were to be controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, where do you see the word "control"? I'm talking about restrictions, Mr. Brown. Why are you misrepresenting my words? I am here talking about a soft border, not control. And in doing so I mentioned the examples of the European practice and the boarders between Alsace and Lorraine.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read it here that: "... we'll never allow the border running along Serbian territories to become real restrictive, although that was the case for a while because of the situation ... economic relationship was such that it had to be imposed, but things will change." One could read that as, "We don't want a border between Serbian lands, Serbian territories." Maybe that echos what you said about the Posavina corridor. It wasn't just important to have the Posavina Corridor because it linked all the territories in Bosnia, but it was important because if you control Posavina, you were able to link the Serb territories in Croatia, the Serb territories in Bosnia, to Serbia itself. So maybe this is another example that we shouldn't have borders between Serb lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you only this: Does it say here that the border shouldn't be a restrictive one, or does it say that we should unite with Serbia? So not to be a restrictive one, or do we unite?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It deals with the borders. Those borders between Serb territories were not to be restrictive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic said at the Assembly session, and he agreed with me, that neither on the Una or the Drina any passports would be required and that there wouldn't be any restrictions? Have you ever come across this statement of his?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the two time-lines admitted into evidence. We might as well tender the video-clip, but we don't have the time to show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, what is your observation as to the video-clip itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to see the video-clip. I think - I may be wrong - this is one of the exhibits we got late notice of for use today. I don't -- I don't object to these pages going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit those two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1934, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll definitely play the video in the future once we have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your paragraph 2.35, Mr. Brown, persist in suggesting that the target of military operations were populated places, that is to say civilians rather than the Muslim and the Croat armed forces. Is that right? Please look at your paragraph 2.35. [In English] [As read] "In Sanski Most, for example, in late May against the Muslim and Croat inhabited areas were carried out by both 6th Brigade and TO units acting in co-operation." Footnote 322.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you understand this to be an attack on populated places and civilians or an attack on the armed forces deployed there and firing from that area?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible to see the footnote reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the amalgamated statement of the witness, paragraph 2.35, on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You wanted to see the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- footnote reference 322.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, it's P03313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's upload that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what did you conclude on the basis of this? Did you conclude that the target of the attack was the populated place mentioned here and the civilians, or does this document testify about the existence of armed formations, even those who came from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible to have page 2, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is a four-page document. Could we print it. In the meantime, while the witness is reading the document, let us print it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In item 2 can you see that there is a request for the enemy forces to be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that would seem to echo the disarmament operations that were going on in other municipalities around at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the strength of the Muslim forces deployed in Vrhpolje, Kamengrad, Hrustovo, and other villages around Sanski Most? Do you know their numbers, including those in the very centre of Sanski Most called Mahala?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the details of the -- of -- of any armed groups in those areas, but I do know that the area was taken control very quickly after shelling and operations by the TO of Sanski Most and the 6th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that we tolerated their existence up to the point when they launched offensives? And the Muslims themselves are writing this in a book, where they say we decided to go on the offensive, we clashed with them, and we were defeated. Do you know that we tolerated their existence until the 7th of May? For nearly seven weeks of the war we didn't do anything against them because we didn't know what they had at their disposal. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the take-over of Sanski Most by Serbian authorities occurred in the middle to late April, and I'm not aware of significant offensives in Sanski Most launched by the non-Serb population and that this was tolerated until -- until the 7th of May. I think Sanski Most is one of those municipalities in which power was taken over, I believe, around about the 18th or 19th of April. I may be wrong a little bit on the timings. And it's also one of those municipalities from the documents that seem to fit with this chain of disarmament. And there was an attack around this period after this order was issued which involved artillery from the 6th Brigade, and control of Mahala was taken very quickly. There were follow-on operations in which Serb soldiers, I believe, did die and there were casualties. That would indicate that the area was not completely unarmed. But again, Sanski Most was -- well, the territory was controlled very quickly within the first few days of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So having looked at the document, can you answer the original question put by the accused, i.e., -- I'll read it out: "Do you understand this," the paragraph in your report, "this to be an attack on populated placed and civilians or an attack on the armed forces deployed there and firing from that area?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it seems to indicate that it's -- they're couching it as armed -- armed groups in there. There are references to artillery preparation in Mahala and other areas, settlements. It may well be that it's both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break, Mr. Karadzic, for 25 minutes. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before we take the break, could I ask the Defence for a copy of the map, the excerpt which they put on the ELMO, which was represented as being part of some kind of "Glas" compilation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take a break for --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have a coloured version from books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for 25 minutes and resume at ten to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that before the attack on the Mahala, which was executed by the Serb army in order to deal with the terrorist -- terrorists, it was communicated by radio that all civilians should move to the stadium for the duration of combat?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to refer you to the testimony of Witness Zulic who described it. Do you know that from the places of Hrustovo and others the army actually protected civilians and took them to Tomina, which was in the same municipality? They were simply taken away for the duration of the fights, and they were accommodated in a different part of the municipality in some Muslim houses in Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. And if that's what the witness says, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to refer you to the statement of (redacted) She described how she was taken to Tomina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at P3601.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You must know who Colonel Basara was, because you mentioned him. He was commander of the 6th Brigade in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, I'd like to ask you this: Did you know that at a certain point in your report you mentioned that brigades were brought in, the 6th Brigade, for example, which was brought to Sanski Most and the 43rd Brigade to Prijedor. Did you know that these municipalities were the home municipalities of those brigades or did you think they were brought in because of some special reason, other reason?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I am aware that that was the areas that those brigades came from. But at the time they were redeployed, they were in operations in Western Slavonia. The whole of the 43rd Brigade didn't deploy back to Prijedor, only a part of it. And in essence they were taken out of combat in Western Slavonia to go back to those areas in Prijedor and Sanski Most. But, yes, I'm aware that the brigades were from that area. They weren't sent back, as I am aware, to be stood down or demobilised, but that they were tasked to control the territory; Prijedor in the case of the 43rd Brigade, and Sanski Most in the case of the 6th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see this document, and did you refer to it in your report? It is a document by Colonel Basara. Have a look at item 1. He orders that the soldiers who were undisciplined and recalcitrant should be sent away. He also orders that all soldiers prone to committing genocide against people unable to conduct an armed struggle must be discharged, et cetera. Have you seen this document previously?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'd have to check my footnotes, Mr. Karadzic. There are lot of documents in the report, and it's been some time since I've looked at it, so I'd have to check. Maybe I can do that this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page. I haven't found any reference of yours to this document. Have a look at item 6. Do you agree, as an officer, that the 6th Brigade commander undertook preventive measures and that he prohibited certain activities and threatened with sanctioning any potential perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the document does seem to indicate that. I have seen, in fairness, a couple of other documents from the corps indicating that they will take similar sanctions. But as I said earlier on, I don't think I saw too many examples where sanctions were -- were indeed taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can only regretfully note that, Mr. Brown, but the Chamber did observe that not a single incident was left that was not sanctioned sooner or later. In any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Completely untrue statement from Mr. Karadzic on the Chamber observing that not a single incident was ever left unsanctioned. Completely untrue from the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just put your question and reserve your submission for a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not include this document in your report in any case, did you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may not have. I don't know where this document's from, so it may well be that it didn't find its way in there. If I'd seen it, I would probably have referenced it. As I said, I think some of the limitations of the report at the beginning is that it didn't include every single document. But if I had seen this one, I would most likely have made reference to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was in the possession of the OTP, and it was tendered by P3601. Can we next have -- well, let me draw your attention to paragraph 2, item 100 -- 2.100. In that paragraph you discuss Kljuc and that certain people there were released after questioning initially, and by the 2nd of June, 1992, while some 900 people had been detained: [In English] "The same report also noted that, because Muslim extremists had failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village in Prnjavor municipality had been 'expelled.'" [Interpretation] Did you know that there were almost 19.000 Muslims living in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the figures of Kljuc in terms of -- in terms of population. I know there were a lot, but I don't know the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 27th of May there were at least five or more synchronised attacks by the Muslim Green Berets on the Serb police, military, and civilians and that there were a number of casualties?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of an incident in Kljuc in and around the time of the disarmament operations which was the ambush of a bus containing soldiers of the JNA who I believe were coming back from Knin in which a number were killed. There may also, either in that attack or a different attack, have been a mine placed on the road. I believe I referenced that somewhere in the report. So I don't doubt that there certainly was that incident. There may have been others that I'm unaware of. But there was an incident in Kljuc in which, I think, two or maybe more JNA soldiers were killed and a number injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Taking into account that there were at least five armed attacks which you called incidents and that out of the 19.000 Muslims 900 were captured, does it resemble an attack on the Muslim community to you, or was it a result of fighting, during which process the enemy soldiers were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my understanding that the -- let me step back. It was my understanding that operations were planned in Kljuc and that this incident occurred and that the -- the operation in Kljuc was not solely in response to -- to the -- to the attack on the coach. There was a similar incident, for example, in Prijedor. A number of soldiers were killed, and yet in Prijedor there had been this disarmament plan being planned and put into operation. Yes, I believe this document, I have to go back to it again, 900 were captured. Kljuc was taken over again very quickly within a couple of days. I would have expected that if 900 individuals were armed and defending Kljuc that it would have taken longer than a day or two to -- to take control of the territory. I believe a large number of people in Kljuc subsequently left the municipality. So what I observed in Kljuc was not that there was a large defensive force in which the -- the Bosnian Serb or the VRS engaged in protracted conflict. What I observed in there, and also in Sanski Most and Prijedor, for that matter, was that there was a plan to disarm. The territories were taken over very quickly. There were some Serb casualties. There had been some potentially provocative incidents. The areas were not completely unarmed, but that Serb casualties, in essence, were relatively light. The territories were taken very quickly, often with large numbers of people being taken into captivity or custody and moved between various centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Brown, did you take note of the fact that Kljuc was populated by Serbs and that they were in the majority and that not the whole of Kljuc was captured but, rather, it involved a few Muslim villages which had fighters? There was no fighting in the town itself but in the village of Velagic and others surrounding Kljuc. And that as of the 6th of April, when the conflict broke out, until the 20th of May, they were left alone. No one touched them.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were problem in Kljuc in early May. I know that's referenced in some documents as well, and I believe -- I'd have to check my reference, but I'm -- I'm -- I believe there was an incident in -- in the first few days in Kljuc in which a non-Serb or some non-Serbs were killed. There clearly was ethnic tensions in Kljuc. There was discussion amongst military commanders about what was happening in there and that that territory needed to be controlled. And I place the events in Kljuc alongside the similar events in Sanski Most and Prijedor. In order to take control of that territory, a disarmament operation was undertaken. It may well have been that in Kljuc, Velagic, Pudin Han, for example, is another one, were the scene of operations, but I believe that other operations took place later in June in order to completely secure the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I will now dispute that by showing the following facts: In the valley of the Sana River, in Prijedor, in Sanski Most, and Kljuc, towards the end of May there were synchronised Muslim attacks on Serb soldiers and civilians. Following that, the Serb army undertook operations. Isn't that correct? Do you recall Hambarine on the 22nd of May, Kozarac on the 24th of May, and on the 27th May the rest of the municipalities? Prijedor, on the other hand, was attacked by the Green Berets on the 30th of May. Is that correct or is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I can break your question up by firstly saying: I've admitted in the report and I've already admitted earlier on that there were a number of incidents in some of those municipalities in which Serb soldiers were killed. But if you look at the chain of events as we discussed last week, that plans of operations in order to disarm and to take control of territory were in operation well before some of those incidents occurred. And there's a reference, for example, in the Prijedor documentation that a plan was underway and it was due to take place, I believe, on the 22nd but that an incident in Hambarine at a check-point at which some soldiers were killed in essence stopped that plan. So it's not that in -- somehow in those municipalities that these flash-point incidents occurred and it was because of that that the territory -- that these military operations took place and the territory was controlled and large numbers of people were rounded up. I would argue that a plan -- plans had already been implemented through the chain that we talked about last week and that either as a result of that planning, or separately, flash-point incidents did occur in which soldiers were killed. I accept that Prijedor, for example, on the 30th of May was attacked and a small group of non-Serbs killed some individuals, I think on the approaches to Prijedor, but the response to that was very swift in Prijedor. Within a very short space of time, not even a day, I believe, was -- control was taken over in the town. I think they attacked the -- either the police station or a hotel there. But irrespective, yes, there were flash-point incidents, yes, a number of soldiers appeared to have been killed, but for me those were not the reason that those municipalities were taken over and that operations were conducted. It was already planned that these disarmament operations and controls were due to be undertaken. And furthermore, the fact that in Prijedor within a day or two the Krajina Corps are announcing that thousands of people had been sent to Trnopolje and Omarska does not give me the impression that it was simply the flash-point incidents in Hambarine and Kozarac that were the reason for those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would kindly ask you to narrow down your answers. Did you know that in all three municipalities the Serb authorities were formed, whereas an offer was made to the Muslims to establish their or -- their own municipalities? For example, the Muslims did initiate the origins of their own municipalities, say, in Sanski Most and Kljuc. That is the underlying question of mine. Did you know about that or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware, and maybe not of the details, that there were negotiations in Kljuc -- sorry, in Sanski Most in particular, prior to control being taken over in the middle to late April. In relation to Prijedor, I know that the control was taken in that municipality at the end of April, 30th of April, and that involved use of the TO and the police and awareness of the -- by the 34th -- 43rd Brigade. So maybe there was negotiations, I don't know, in the spring -- in the spring months, but I do know by the end of April that control had been taken over, i.e., political control, I guess, had been taken over in -- in those municipalities. In all three, actually - Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know why there was a take-over in Prijedor without fighting? Did you know that there was an order from Sarajevo that the JNA and Serbs in Prijedor be attacked and that the message was intercepted? That is why the take-over took place, to prevent the attack from happening.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would isolate Prijedor from what was going on in the other municipalities. In the end of March, at the Assembly sessions there, there was a decision to form Crisis Staffs. There was a decision to establish TOs. I would see the take-over of power in those municipalities in April more related to what was happening in the Assembly sessions in the middle and late March 1992 and the desire to control that territory. I don't know of any order from Sarajevo that the JNA and Serbs were to be attacked. I haven't seen that. But I would -- bearing in mind the pattern that seemed to happen in the middle of April to late April and into May, many of the municipalities were taken over. And I see that more in line with the instructions that were passed out at the Assembly sessions at the end of March 1992 in relation to Crisis Staffs and the TO and taking control of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you seem to be guessing a lot, and you don't know of this key element of this telegram sent from the Ministry of Defence and of the interior explaining the decision of the Muslim-Croat Presidency to attack the JNA and Serbs. This was already something that was shown in the courtroom and yet you are ignorant of the fact. Even after the event we still proposed to them that they create their own municipalities in Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Kljuc. So how was it that we wanted all the territory and yet at the same time we proposed they make their own municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is I haven't seen the document. If you want to show it to me, I'm more than happy to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but I have no time. You should have been aware of it. This report without this key element does not stand. You say that the Muslim population was expelled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you put your statement or question, let the witness answer it. Would you like to comment on the comments by Mr. Karadzic that your report does not stand without this key element?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no -- no comment on that, sir. I think the report, I hope, stands on the documents that I was able to see and review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, refrain from making unnecessary comments. That takes up -- will take up more time, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But -- very well. I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Brown, that you cannot establish a pattern of behaviour of the Serb army without knowing about the activities of the Muslim side? Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I agree that there may be limitations in the report without all the information from the non-Serb side, but I believe, looking at the documents from the Krajina Corps, that I can establish a pattern within the limitations of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no time to further verify this position of yours. Let's look at paragraph 2.100. There you say that the civilians of Lisnja were expelled. We checked the document you referred to, which is 65 ter number 545.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please upload it. I believe there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You seem to refer to the document, so you must have had a translation. Look at item 2, the second part: [As read] "During fighting around Prijedor, some 900 people were taken prisoner and about 400 rifles were seized. In the area of Prijedor the situation is under control and there is no large-scale fighting. The fighting in the area of Sanski Most is unchanged. In the area of Derventa there continues to be occasional artillery fire, well, because Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons. The Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." Oh, here we have the translation. So probably it's not an error on your part. Mr. Brown, they were neither expelled nor resettled. They were simply moved out of the area. Do you see a difference between the three terms?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say what is stated in the document, that they have been expelled. The Krajina Corps would have put that in. I would have thought they would have put "resettled" or "happily moved out" if it was different. But it references "expelled." It would seem to indicate, at least from this document, that the Muslims in that village were no longer living there due to the fact that extremists or Muslim extremists hadn't handed in their weapons, presumably in relation to the disarmament operations that were going on around that time. I think the document seems to speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in the area of Derventa there is artillery fire and the army moved out the Muslim population. Do you know that in accordance with the law on total national defence there is an obligation to evacuate the civilian population while there is fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I wouldn't link -- as far as I'm aware, Lisnja village is in Prnjavor municipality and not Derventa. I'm not sure linking the two is -- is necessarily accurate. I know there was fighting in Derventa at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is it your argument that the last sentence of para 2 in this document wrongly translated? Because the document says: "The Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a mistranslation, and it completely changes the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your reading of B/C/S was translated as "expelled." So we'll check it later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let the interpreters tell you now whether there's a difference between "expelled." "Proterano," "preseljeno," "iseljeno," these three terms, "expelled," "resettled," "moved out," is there a difference? Is there a difference between these three concepts and is there a difference in the scale involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you read out the last sentence of para 2 in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the area of Derventa there is still artillery fire from time to time, while in the area of the village of Lisnja, due to the fact that Muslim extremists did not surrender their weapons, the Muslim population was moved out." That's it, "moved out."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would stand by my assessment of the situation, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I may want to follow up on that, Your Honour, because I recall that previously I had an interpreter look carefully at this passage to see what the word was and it was reported to me that it was "expelled," but we'll look at that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You deal with that in paragraph 2.155. Isn't that right? There is another reference to this paragraph and to the corps. [In English] [Previous translation continued] "... after the attack [sic] by units of the 1st Krajina Corps on Lisnja, the Corps reported that the entire population of the village -- of that village had been expelled." [Interpretation] So now you say that it was done by the 1st Corps, and this could have been done by the civilian authorities. Isn't that right? Because the civilian protection is duty-bound to move the population while the fighting is still going on. Where do you find this, that it was done by the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to check maybe some other references. I may be prepared to amend it based on this document alone. I'd have to look at other ones. It's reported in the 1st Krajina Corps reports, so it presumably is of importance to them. And the paragraph starts with, The 1st Krajina Corps units are still holding the same positions, and then goes into detail about the areas that the corps are working in. I can look at it again. Maybe if I need to amend it, I'm more than happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that according to our law this is a legal requirement, according to our law on total national defence, evacuation of the civilian population, announcing bombing, ultimatums, and so on? Isn't all of that in accordance with the laws, so the civilians would know what lies ahead and that they be given enough time to seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't make that clear in this document, Mr. Karadzic. It doesn't indicate that for their own safety, you know, in accordance with the law, in order to minimise civilian casualties. It doesn't make reference to that at all. I wouldn't necessarily put this particular incident in isolation either. I don't know the law that you're referring to, and I would be interested to look at it, but I -- my reading of this is not that these individuals are somehow being moved out for -- for their own safety, bearing in mind at the same time what was happening in other municipalities in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, please explain this to me: How are you going to identify unlawful conduct on the part of the 1st Krajina Corps if you're not familiar with the law on the basis of which they are waging war?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure of the question. I'm not a lawyer. What I'm saying is what I see in a regular combat report from the corps in early June and that's what's reported. It seems to fit what was happening in other municipalities around the same time, and it in particular adds to my assessment that there were operations which came through the authorities to conduct operations in order to disarm that resulted in a large number of people in those municipalities either being attacked or moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a brief question. Do you know or do you agree -- have you identified the following, rather, that it was the police that was in charge of disarming until the first soldiers started losing their lives and that the army got involved only at the end of May when they started firing at the army? Just yes or no. Did you identify that? Did you realise that the army was not interfering until the soldiers actually started getting killed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that initially the disarmament operations, as articulated through the ARK municipalities, initially tasked the MUP to deal with that but that that changed in and around the middle of May. And I do not see that that was linked to individual soldiers being killed at that time. In essence it seems that the hardening or the involvement of the military came round the middle of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, sir, Mr. Brown, when the soldiers get fired at by their own civilian population from behind their backs, is it not perfectly legitimate for the army to get involved at that point?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem legitimate for the army to conduct security operations if they're being fired at. But bearing in mind that what was going on in the Krajina seemed to have occurred in other municipalities outside the Krajina, I don't see this as somehow some localised security operation in which a number of minor incident -- relatively minor, unfortunate, clearly, for the soldiers who were injured or killed, minor operations in which those incidents happened and the army were taking appropriate security measures in order to deal with those individuals who may have conducted that type of attack. It would seem that, you know, if you look at Prijedor, the 1st Krajina Corps documents at the end of May had thousands of people rounded up and placed in Omarska and Trnopolje. If it was a security operation targeted against sporadic -- unfortunate sporadic incidents against soldiers, I wouldn't necessarily -- that wouldn't necessarily necessitate the rounding up of, you know, 7.000 individuals, or whatever is annotated in the documents at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, it's not 7.000. It's less than 3.000. Secondly, sir, this happened, isn't that right, only after the 30th of May, after the attack at Prijedor? And thirdly, you claim that these are individuals that attacked, not armed units. Are you saying that in Krajina there were armed Muslim individuals, or is what I am saying the truth, that even before the war, in all the 103 municipalities that are there, they had a unit and a staff of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to that compound question. I mean, I haven't been objecting, but these are getting huge and complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you break down, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you claim that these were individuals rather than armed formations? As you said on line 11, page 73. Transcript. Transcript. Line 11, page 73.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there may well have been armed groups. I'm not aware of the details of all activities from the Muslim side in many of these municipalities. I do know, for example, in the corridor that there was shelling from over the Croatian side. I'm aware that some of the municipalities in the corridor took control and that they were -- they seeped to be quite well armed. There may well have been the planning. There may well have been a desire. There may well have been some groups that were more than just individuals. But it did seem to me that the -- whatever armed groups may have been present in some of those municipalities, that they weren't particularly effective. Yes, there were these low -- lowish-level incidents in which some Serbs soldiers were killed, but they certainly didn't stop much at all. And, for example, when I wrote a report in relation to Prijedor and tried to look at this issue, it seemed in comparison that whatever defensive organisation may have been present in Prijedor, it was relatively rudimentary. It didn't seem particularly well structured or organised. It didn't appear to be particularly well armed. They may well have had small arms. They may well have had some explosives and mines and some were maybe hand-held rocket launchers, but it certainly didn't stop the VRS at all. And in comparison, the VRS was able to call on significant assets, including the most up-to-date tanks, artillery, well-seasoned troops that had spent a significant amount of time fighting in Croatia, and that whatever defensive structures or whatever armed structures were in those municipalities certainly weren't particularly effective. It may well have been there had been a desire by non-Serbs to protect their territories and to arm themselves, but it didn't seem to me to be particularly effective, let alone particularly well structured, certainly in comparison to what the VRS were able to call on and the assets they had at their disposal. And it seemed that in many of those municipalities in the Krajina, where operations did take place, they were over relatively quickly, maybe with follow-up operations in the subsequent weeks and months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Brown, how long your answer is to my simple question. Do you know of the war preparations of the Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know about the establishment of the Patriotic League consisting of 103 municipal staffs and municipal brigades?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a point, Mr. Karadzic. I can't answer your questions, often, in a simpler way because there is usually some context behind it. Where I can, I will answer in a simple manner. In relation to the Patriotic League, I'm not aware of it. I did not look at the issue of the Patriotic League. That was not part of the report. It didn't come out necessarily in detail through the 1 Krajina Corps documents. It may well have been that the -- obviously there was an ABiH at some stage. Mr. Izetbegovic mobilised the TO, and there was -- I believe, Croatian troops had come over the border in some places in Bosnia, but it wasn't a part of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brown, you are assessing what the 1st Krajina Corps did. And if you don't know what kind of challenges they were up against, if you don't know what kind of problems they were up against, how can you assess the 1st Krajina Corps without knowing what they had been dealing with?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I'm -- I do flag up in the report some of the problems that the 1st Krajina Corps faced. I don't deny that the 1st Krajina Corps suffered casualties through the -- 1992. I don't deny that the Krajina Corps had a long border in which it was often at the contact point conducting quite tough fighting, certainly on the Central Bosnia area. To a degree there was harrying from artillery in Croatia. So I don't doubt that. But it seems that the municipality attacks that occurred in May and June and in, to some extent, into July, that those municipality attacks were over relatively quickly and that control was taken relatively quickly and the operations that they continued through that -- through the summer were relatively minor. I don't doubt on the contact points that the Krajina Corps was fighting, you know, quite a determined opponent, but that's not what I was looking at. I was looking at some of the municipality attacks. And it seems that in comparison to the -- whatever defensive forces were there or whatever armed groups were there, that -- that control was taken very quickly by General Talic, and it would seem that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you dealt with the in-depth fighting carried out by the 1st Krajina Corps, not fighting at the front line itself. Do you claim that it was the 1st Krajina Corps that attacked Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc, or do you agree with me that first it was the Muslim formations from Kljuc, Prijedor, and Sanski Most attacked the Serbs as civilians and the police as well, and once they attacked the army, they got a military response? I claim that they were the first to attack, and you are talking about attacks in municipalities. We have quite a few documents, but let us get this straight. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my claim that elements of the 1st Krajina Corps were involved in operations in Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc and that those operations took place after control had been seized in April, predominantly, 1992, and that these operations, in order to secure that territory, those operations were undertaken initially under the -- the umbrella of disarming extremist groups or paramilitary groups, and those particularly were located in non-Serb villages. And I didn't see examples of 1st Krajina Corps units operating outside non-Serb villages in order to disarm the population. I do concede that during those operations that there were instances, and it may even be in one or two cases prior to those, there were incidents where Serb soldiers were killed, but it was not that the Serb soldiers were attacked and therefore that was a justification for those operations. I would argue control had been taken. That in order to secure control of those municipalities, disarmament operations were planned and operated. And those operations were successful. They were conducted by components of the corps, often in conjunction with the police. And that that territory was part of the territory that was deemed to be Serb or that they wanted to control and that the control of that -- of those areas was effected very quickly, and there was continuing operations after that. Concurrently with that, there was an operation -- a number of large-scale operations that the Krajina Corps were involved in, in particular Operation Corridor, but obviously operations in other areas, including Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are dealing with what the subject that you wrote about was, the fighting far away from the front line. This is what I put to you, that the army did not interfere with disarmament or fighting until it was attacked. Yes or no? Is it correct that it was first the Muslims that attacked the army in Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with your position, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. That will do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1353. Could we please have a look at that now. D1353.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Krupa, Bosanska Krupa, in your report, and now we are going to see what the instructions on the evacuation of the population are like, and this has to do with refugees from the local commune of Arapusa. Did you have this document in your possession?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I did, or I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can read the page in English, and I'm going to tell you what this is all about. Arapusa is a Muslim village, and some other Muslims from Bosanska Krupa fled to Arapusa. Once the fighting for Arapusa started, instructions were issued to evacuate the population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the next page. In English it's fine, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this population was evacuated within Republika Srpska itself. And then it says in this last bullet point that on the basis of the agreement reached between Mr. Vjestica and the commander at the moment when peace is established, the command is duty-bound to ensure the safe return of the population to Arapusa, to their homes there, and the refugees to Bosanska Krupa. Did you see who all the signatories are, Emir Sabic, a Muslim, and another Muslim, Fuad. And, down here, for the commander of the battalion, it was signed by Bozo Erceg and Djordje Jez. Evacuation within the same municipality and the same republic, is that ethnic cleansing or is this an operation envisaged by law?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say the context behind this evacuation. It may well have been that operations, combat operations, were going on at that time and that those who signed it were under the impression that they were going to be allowed back and that was genuine. It may well have been a distinct possibility that those individuals signed it through fear or under the misapprehension that they were going to be allowed back and that in fact this was a ruse to in -- order them to leave. I don't know. All I can say is that Mr. Vjestica, not long after this, seemed to be under the impression that those Muslims in Bosanska Krupa would not be returning. So I don't know the details of why this document was signed or -- or how it came to be signed, whether those signatories did it through force, misapprehension, or a genuine belief that they were going to be allowed to return at that time. It would seem to me that two weeks later Mr. Vjestica is not saying words that would seem to echo the sentiment of this document, and in fact quite the contrary, that these people were not going to be allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, he said that they were not there, that they wouldn't be there for as long as the fighting is going on, and he expressed his doubt as to their return. So you're not reading documents properly. Did the OTP put this document at your disposal and did you just eliminate it on your own?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have to object to this argumentative comment that he's not reading documents properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time, Mr. Karadzic, you should know the rules. Refrain from making unnecessary statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Witness, haven't you read Vjestica's words yourself? They will not be there for as long as the fighting is going on. Did you not read that out on the 18th? His words were: "They will not be there until the fighting goes on."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that in this document or is it in the Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you quoted, that Vjestica said, and that's what you read out, on the 18th. "They will not be there while the fighting is going on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While witness is reading that document, Mr. Tieger, did you say you would need five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, just 60 seconds at most, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vjestica says: "Will they have a place to return to? I think it unlikely after our president has told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, sir, he is anticipating that they were not going to live in the Serbian entity, not that somebody was going to prohibit them from doing so. Secondly, do you know that these people were relocated within Republika Srpska, not outside of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of where these individuals were relocated. It may well have been that they were moved over the river. I'm -- but I'm not aware of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your microphone. Yes, it's now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, it was possible to determine by localities that they were moving inside Republika Srpska and they even went to Sanski Most. What we have here is the municipality of Krupa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask whether this 65 ter 545 has been admitted into evidence, the one that speaks about the village of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that has been already admitted, Exhibit P3927.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, should we adjourn for today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, but I kindly ask you to reconsider the issue of time. This is the summary of the entire indictment, or almost of the entire indictment. Seven hours is by far too little. With any other witness I would have been given seven days at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, as I told you earlier today, that we decided to interpose another witness's evidence with you, my anticipation is that we may be able to resume your evidence around 11.30 tomorrow morning. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It -- if we can briefly move into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If my memory's correct, the Defence didn't take any position with respect to that. Mr. Robinson? If necessary, we'll go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we can do this in public session. We didn't oppose that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.
